commenti.body:
I just saw it and thought it was great.

I think most people imagined/ hoped it would turn into Joker breaking free and starting some kind of crime spree.

Instead we got a sequel to the first movie. Showing a continuation of the hapless and mentally ill Aurther, unable to to control events as they spiral out of control around him. There was never going to be a happy ending for him.

I think the musical elements helped relieve what otherwise was an incredibly bleak story.

> As this happened, I also fell out of love with Arthur, just like Harley Quinn did a couple of minutes before, after all I prefer the chaotic, dangerous clown, not the heartbroken, wimpy, abused loser. This made me reflect upon my own feelings, that the most lovable part of a person is their dark side. That I only cared about Arthur's life as long as I was led to believe that I'm witnessing the origins of the clown of chaos, batman's arch enemy. When it was revealed to me that he's not that, my emotions ceased in a second, and now I was feeling what I was judging Harley Quinn for a couple minutes ago. The theme of the movie truly was shadow integration.

I fail to follow your logic. You understood that following the story of a boring wimpy abused loser is not as fun as a following one of Batman's arch enemy and that made you realize that a person's "dark side" is their most loveable part?

We only cared about Arthur's story as long as we were under the impression that it's the origin story of Joker. And when it was revealed to us that he is not the Joker, we stopped caring about him, his story, and the whole movie. Ergo, we cared about him because of his "dark side", or in other words, his shadow made him interesting in the first place.

What does this have to do with his "dark side"? You'd experience the same feelings if you learned that Sarah Connor is just a random waitress, Thomas Anderson isn't the One and Peter Parker isn't Spiderman.

This is an excellent breakdown. To extend on the idea: "The Joker" is sort of more an ideal, almost an entity, something that lives vicariously through the dark side and shadow self of others. Arther was like the precursor, the first human representation of this darkness within us all. And then it festered and grew with everything you put down here.

Arthur's story is a damned tragedy, and it's a tragedy that the audience is disillusioned by him as well. His compassion and kindness sucked out of him, society "created" him with all of these environmental and external pressures. He succumbed. But the evil lives on, having gained energy through his spirit and the spirit of the mob. And now will fully manifest into a terror that is the canonical Joker.

Masterpiece.

Excellent breakdown OP. Can't stand to see the lack of upvotes or intelligent conversation. People in real life, much like the prison guards, become irritated when a light is illuminated on uncomfortable truths that do not align with their fantasy of how things "should be"

And the directors etc. are incredibly brave for putting forth the story like this, unapologetically. I'm getting the chills right now from the incredible storytelling and subversion of expectations done correctly.

Thank you for saying so. 

The fans' reaction is very interesting, I've even seen some threads suggesting that the prison guards "raped the Joker out of Arthur" and that this was meant as a jab at the fans for idolizing a chaotic character. 

The movie feels too brave to me to believe that the studio only made it for the purposes of generating revenue. If you think about it, they made a solid art film out of a superhero franchise, what a strange thing to do...

Damn. I do think it was a symbolic "raping the Joker out of Arthur" but not so sure it was a jab at fans. It was more just an example of the perversion within society that led to the creation of the real Joker. Too brave, for sure. And I am here for it :)

Many times, art pieces are meant to sort of simmer on the collective psyche a bit, and have some introspective moments about ourselves and how we relate to the characters' downfall. This can be painful.
I just watched joker in the cinema and love your perspective. I was surprised at the amount of negative reviews and was glad to see someone with a familiar positive view. Thanks for sharing. :)
Yes totally Agree!! The music was great and I think jazz really suites lady Gaga.

Yeah I adored it and it's breaking my brain seeing everyone say it was boring or miserable or 'too happy that's not the joker I know!!!' whatever else they are saying....it was deep social commentary about the police system, how we view hero's and villains, WHY hero's and villains are so popular despite just masking real societal problems....

Art is meant to disturb the comfortable and comfort the disturbed.

I'm not arguing it couldn't have been shorter or executed better, I don't agree but that's a different discussion to the message of the film. But as someone who is mentally ill and has been left behind by the underfunded healthcare system, and had relationships where I or they wanted an idealised version of the other and not the true person, I related so much to it.

This is exactly why they churn out the same movie out year after year after year. Ok fine just make Batman V Superman V idk, Godzilla again. I don't care anymore.

Desirable might have been better word choice. Arthur and Joker are both one person who haven’t been integrated. The Joker only comes out of Arthur after years of him suppressing any and all dark tendencies or beliefs he held. No one went to see the first movie because they knew who Arthur was or that 90% of the movie would have him as the focus. Being an origin story I think some of this was expected, but people went to see it because they love the Joker and all of the bad shit that the Joker brings. It’s no secret the kinds of people who live vicariously through the Joker, the kind of people who love and desire the Joker. Point is, feeling utterly let down by a story about some boring wimpy loser is evident of the viewer not really desiring or loving Arthur in the sense you may have thought you felt after the first movie. Being unable to realize you only love Arthur for his dark tendencies after viewing the new movie is you failing to realize you only love the Joker and you never loved Arthur in the way Arthur wishes to be loved by others. You, the viewer, wishes for Arthur to be something he doesnt wish to be and struggles to integrate. Failing to portray this idea was by no means a failure of the director, it’s a failure of the viewer to understand this if the viewer fails to integrate their own shadow. 

If you truthfully believe Arthur’s dark tendencies aren’t “lovable” in the way it’s being used, then it makes absolutely no sense why you believe Arthur is “boring”or “wimpy” or that the story was “not fun”. You should be overjoyed with Arthur not wishing to be the Joker and how the movie ends. After all, he is a murderer (dark tendency?), so why aren’t you happy with the way the film ends?

I think using the terms "desirable" or "loveable" to describe why someone might prefer the joker over arthur is being rather obtuse.

The reason people like the psychotic side of Arthur more isn't because we're attracted to murder or arson, it's because from a viewer's perspective it is far more ***entertaining*** to watch someone go off the rails and commit unthinkable acts rather than watch someone simply cave in to pain and despair. And that is really what it comes down to. 

Everyone knows full well what it is to watch someone hurt themselves or be hurt, and sure, there are ways to depict such a story that can be interesting or thought provoking. But how many people do you know that take pleasure in starting fires? Robbing banks? Representing themselves in court wearing clown makeup for their 5 count murder trial? Which is more interesting, exciting and new? We shouldn't be surprised that the things we simply don't know much about are more exciting to learn about or see. "*What could possibly make someone do that?*"

I think the two movies depicting the origin story of the figure that would inspire a more comic accurate joker is definitely an interesting twist, however I think this post fails to understand why the reception to the movie isn't as grand as it is. And I did like it, though I like thinking about it more than I liked watching it as the singing scenes were just too much for me, I've never been a big fan of musicals.

I don't think claiming it's about "shadow integration" is even accurate either, seeing as throughout the entire movie the only person that never believed that Arthur was any different from "the joker" seemed to be Arthur himself. Everyone else believed he was either ill or idolised into something he never was.
